title: 04 — Cores, Threads and Concurrency
html:
04 — Cores, Threads and Concurrency

The one idea: Polars already uses every core for one query. Your job is not to add parallelism but to stop fighting it: size its thread pool to the cores you really have, overlap waiting with collect_async, and reach for processes only for work Polars can't run itself.

1. What it is

Tool What it does
POLARS_MAX_THREADS Size of Polars' thread pool. Read once, when polars is imported
pl.thread_pool_size() The size actually in use
collect_async() Run a lazy query on Polars' threads and await it from asyncio
collect(background=True) Start a query and get a handle to fetch the result later
ProcessPoolExecutor with spawn Separate processes, for Python code that holds the GIL
POLARS_ENGINE_AFFINITY Default engine (streaming or in-memory) 
---
title: Choosing the kind of concurrency
---
flowchart TB
    Q{"What is slow?"} -->|"Polars query"| A["Nothing to add:<br/>one query uses all cores"]
    Q -->|"Waiting (APIs, DB, cloud reads)"| B["asyncio + collect_async"]
    Q -->|"Pure Python step<br/>(a single-threaded library)"| C["Processes with spawn,<br/>POLARS_MAX_THREADS=1 per worker"]
    Q -->|"Many small files"| D["One scan over a glob,<br/>not a loop of reads"]

2. Why it matters

  • Containers: os.cpu_count() reports the host's cores, not your CPU limit. A pod limited to 2 CPUs on a 64-core node will start 64 threads and thrash.
  • Oversubscription: 4 worker processes × 4 Polars threads on 4 cores means 16 threads competing for 4 cores. Results come out the same, just slower.
  • fork deadlocks: forking a process while Polars holds an internal lock copies the lock in its locked state. Use spawn.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Size the pool once, before import

POLARS_MAX_THREADS=2 python job.py         # in a container limited to 2 CPUs

In Kubernetes, set it from the CPU limit (for example through the Downward API, or a fixed value in the deployment). Setting it after import polars has no effect.

3.2 Async for overlapping waits

collect_async frees the event loop while Polars works, so a web service can keep serving requests, or start several cloud reads at once. It doesn't make a CPU-bound query faster.

3.3 Processes only for Python-bound work

Use ProcessPoolExecutor(mp_context=mp.get_context("spawn")). Give each worker POLARS_MAX_THREADS=1 (in an initializer) so workers × threads ≈ cores. Put all top-level code under if __name__ == "__main__":, because spawn workers re-import your script.

3.4 Parallel sums are not bit-for-bit reproducible

Floating-point addition depends on order, and the order changes with how work is split across threads. Totals can differ in the last digits between runs (about 1e-6 on sums of hundreds of millions here). Round money to its unit, or use Decimal, before comparing, writing reports or hashing results.

4. Working code

The script measures one heavy query with 1, 2 and 4 threads, runs three queries concurrently with collect_async, and speeds up a single-threaded Python step with spawn workers.

import asyncio, hashlib, os, subprocess, sys, time
import multiprocessing as mp
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
import polars as pl

THREAD_TEST = r'''
import time, polars as pl
lf = pl.scan_parquet("data/big.parquet")
best = 1e9
for _ in range(3):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    lf.group_by("account").agg(pl.col("amount").sum(), pl.col("ref").n_unique()).collect()
    best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - t)
print(f"threads={pl.thread_pool_size()}  best of 3: {best:.2f} s")
'''

def thread_scaling():
    # POLARS_MAX_THREADS is read when polars is imported, so each setting needs a fresh process.
    for threads in ["1", "2", "4"]:
        env = {**os.environ, "POLARS_MAX_THREADS": threads}
        print(subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-c", THREAD_TEST], env=env,
                             capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip())

async def three_queries():
    lf = pl.scan_parquet("data/big.parquet")
    queries = [lf.filter(pl.col("account") == a).select(pl.col("amount").sum()) for a in (1, 2, 3)]
    # collect_async hands the work to Polars' thread pool and returns control to the event loop.
    return await asyncio.gather(*(q.collect_async() for q in queries))

def slow_python_step(part: int) -> int:
    # Stand-in for a single-threaded library: hash every reference in pure Python.
    df = pl.read_parquet("data/big.parquet", n_rows=400_000).filter(pl.col("account") % 4 == part)
    return sum(hashlib.sha256(r.encode()).digest()[0] for r in df["ref"].to_list() for _ in range(5))

def init_worker():
    os.environ["POLARS_MAX_THREADS"] = "1"   # 4 workers x 1 thread = 4 cores, no oversubscription

def main():
    print("cores:", os.cpu_count(), "| Polars thread pool:", pl.thread_pool_size())
    thread_scaling()

    t = time.perf_counter()
    results = asyncio.run(three_queries())
    print(f"\nasyncio: 3 queries with collect_async in {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f} s ->",
          [round(r.item(), 2) for r in results])

    t = time.perf_counter()
    serial = [slow_python_step(p) for p in range(4)]
    serial_s = time.perf_counter() - t
    t = time.perf_counter()
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(4, mp_context=mp.get_context("spawn"), initializer=init_worker) as pool:
        parallel = list(pool.map(slow_python_step, range(4)))
    print(f"\nslow Python step: serial {serial_s:.2f} s, 4 spawn workers {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f} s,"
          f" same result: {serial == parallel}")

if __name__ == "__main__":   # required with spawn: workers re-import this file
    main()

Output:

cores: 4 | Polars thread pool: 4
threads=1  best of 3: 17.09 s
threads=2  best of 3: 7.99 s
threads=4  best of 3: 3.85 s

asyncio: 3 queries with collect_async in 0.23 s -> [3025140.0, 2900280.0, 3075420.0]

slow Python step: serial 0.94 s, 4 spawn workers 0.47 s, same result: True

What to notice:

  • 4 threads were about 4.4× faster than 1. The query (sum plus n_unique on text over 30 million rows) parallelises well. Gains flatten once data loading or memory bandwidth is the limit.
  • collect_async ran three filtered queries in a fraction of a second, and the event loop stayed free meanwhile.
  • The Python hashing step ran about 2× faster with 4 spawn workers. It was not 4×, because starting processes and importing Polars in each costs time. Process pools pay off for long-running steps.
  • An earlier version of this script had no __main__ guard. Every spawned worker re-ran the whole script, and the "parallel" step took 153 seconds instead of half a second.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Wrapping Polars calls in a ThreadPoolExecutor to make one query faster. It already uses all cores.
  2. Setting POLARS_MAX_THREADS after import polars.
  3. Default thread count in a CPU-limited container.
  4. multiprocessing with the default fork on Linux. It can deadlock.
  5. No if __name__ == "__main__": guard with spawn.
  6. Comparing float totals exactly between runs or systems.

6. Exercise (1 hour)

  1. Run the thread test with POLARS_MAX_THREADS=8 on a 4-core machine and explain the result.
  2. Replace the asyncio example with three collect(background=True) handles and fetch the results.
  3. Run the process pool without the initializer (so each worker uses all cores) and compare.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. When is POLARS_MAX_THREADS read?
  2. Why can a Polars job be slow in a Kubernetes pod with a 2-CPU limit?
  3. What does collect_async help with, and what doesn't it help with?
  4. Why use spawn rather than fork with Polars?
  5. Why can two runs of the same group_by(...).sum() differ slightly?

Answers

  1. Once, when polars is imported.
  2. It sizes its pool from the host's core count, so many more threads than CPUs compete.
  3. It overlaps waiting and keeps an event loop responsive. It doesn't speed up a CPU-bound query.
  4. Forking a multithreaded process can copy held locks and deadlock the child.
  5. Threads add partial sums in a different order, and floating-point addition isn't associative.
